title: Triad arpeggios
description: Unfold triad tones melodically across inversions and string sets.

cards.back: The chord tones played one after another (R–3–5 or any order/inversion) instead of all at once. Same pitch classes, unfolded in time.

cards.front: How is an arpeggio related to the triad you already spelled?
cards.back: It is that spelling performed melodically. Inversions of the arpeggio simply start on 3 or 5.

cards.front: Why do arpeggios matter for a single-note line?
cards.back: They outline harmony so a line can state the chord without strumming. They bridge “I know the tones” to “I can play through changes.”

cards.front: C major root position on 4–3–2 is 10 9 8. How do you arpeggiate it?
cards.back: Play those frets in sequence ascending and descending, naming R / 3 / 5: C E G.

cards.front: What do first- and second-inversion C major arpeggios start on, and from which shapes?
cards.back: First starts on E from 14 12 13 or 2 0 1 (E G C). Second starts on G from 5 5 5 (G C E).

cards.front: How do you connect arpeggios across the neck?
cards.back: Ascend C E G in one area, then continue to the next higher C you know, still only chord tones. The same three pitch classes repeat in new octaves and sets.

cards.front: How do you hear major vs minor from an arpeggio?
cards.back: Arpeggiate major then minor and listen for the third: C E G vs C E♭ G.

cards.front: Spell and start G major and G minor root-position arpeggios on 4–3–2.
cards.back: G major: G B D from 5 4 3. G minor: G B♭ D from 5 3 3. Name each tone as you play.

cards.front: Over | C | Am | F | G |, what should an eighth-note outline use?
cards.back: Nearby string-set chord tones only — one bar each. No non-chord tones until you add them on purpose.

cards.front: Where can you find a one-octave D major arpeggio besides 4–3–2?
cards.back: On strings 3–2–1 and on 5–4–3. Same pitch classes D F♯ A, different register and fingering.

cards.front: On a static Em, what is a first improvisation limit, then the next step?
cards.back: Use only E G B. Then allow one approach note that resolves to a chord tone.
No. Use them as melody skeletons: the strong notes of a line, not just a drill.
